messages.text: Take {gift_item}. I may not have a trade, but I know how to say thanks.
Here, {gift_item}. Maybe one of us will find the perfect use for it.
Good, {gift_item} worked. See? I can be useful without a workstation.
{tested_villager} liked it? Excellent. I am putting that under possible talents.
Ah. Then my career in advice pauses here. Try {alternative_gift} for {gift_subject}.
{gift_item} was wrong? Let us call it research. {alternative_gift} should work better.
This is why nobody pays me for advice. Try {alternative_gift}.
You came back? Fair. My next guess is {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the job site I have not found yet. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to looking useful before anyone notices, then.

lines.text: Finding the right work is harder when everyone asks if you found it yet.
Work is work. Finding the right work is the tricky part.
A fair chance can look a lot like standing around until the right bell rings.
If you see a spare job site, do mention it kindly.
Waiting for work is still work if you look worried enough.
Where do I fit? Somewhere useful, I hope, preferably before supper.
I once followed the bell hoping it meant opportunity. It meant hurry.
Unemployed jokes are flexible. That is what I keep telling myself.
That was idle talk, and I would know.
People with trades get tasks. People without trades get errands.
A fair chance is easier to ask for than to recognize.
I organized a barrel once. For a moment, everyone thought I had a calling.
I am trying to look useful, not involved.
I remember having no trade, no thoughts, almost no self. You helped with the important one.
I did not know what I would become, but you made sure I could become anything.
Your face is familiar. So is being confused, but this feels different.
I remember waking with empty hands and a head full of broken bells.
I remember you, though I still do not know what to do with the memory.
Thunder shook the village square so hard every loose shutter complained, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked beds, doors, and loose chores after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the village square, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked who still needed help.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have neighbors to check on.
I checked roofs, beds, and unlucky fences for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the water bucket after.
Odd jobs can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the village square, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the village square, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, odd jobs can wait; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the village square still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before beds, doors, and loose chores. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the village square and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the edge of the square, I saw fear run through the village; then I saw courage catch up.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the village square first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the gap between torches and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the village square enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a ready pair of hands between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the village square, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust from the doorways.
I checked beds, doors, and loose chores, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the village square, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a villager which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the village square, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
Odd jobs can wait. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the village square found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the village square. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow from the meeting path and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the village square. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.

pacify.text: Fine. I have enough problems without carrying this one too.
Even without a trade, I know that should be {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
No. I may not have work, but I still have sense.
